passage: I'm Leela, in Abhinav's class. When the football team list went up and his name wasn't on it, a few of us looked at him. He just shrugged. "Whatever. It's a stupid team anyway." All week he said he didn't care. He stopped going to the ground at lunch and sat with his earphones in, looking bored. But yesterday I saw him staying late, kicking a ball against the back wall of the school, again and again, hard. He didn't see me. I don't know what he's really feeling. But it didn't look like not caring.

qa.q: What did Abhinav say when his name wasn't on the list?
qa.a: "Whatever. It's a stupid team anyway."

qa.q: What feeling might Abhinav's "whatever" be hiding?
qa.a: Probably disappointment and hurt; acting bored protects him from showing how much the rejection stung.

qa.q: How could a friend or coach reach Abhinav?
qa.a: Talk to him privately, without calling out the act, and mention the next trials or ways to improve.

qa.q: Why does Leela doubt that Abhinav doesn't care?
qa.a: She saw him kicking the ball hard, alone, after school, which didn't match his bored act.

grounding: It shows, from a classmate's view, a teenager using a show of not caring to shield himself from rejection.

passage:
Week one: Arnab's best friend moved to Bengaluru. When his mother Aparna asked if he was sad, he said, "It's fine. People move. No big deal," and turned up his music.
Week two: He stopped replying to his friend's messages. "Too busy," he said, though he spent evenings lying on his bed, scrolling.
Week four: Aparna found him looking at an old photo of the two of them on a school trip. He put it face down quickly. "It's nothing." She sat on the edge of his bed and said, "It's okay to miss him." Arnab was quiet for a long time. Then: "If I don't care, it doesn't hurt." That night he finally replied to his friend.

qa.q: Where did Arnab's best friend move?
qa.a: To Bengaluru.

qa.q: What does "If I don't care, it doesn't hurt" reveal?
qa.a: Arnab was acting detached to protect himself from the pain of missing his friend.

qa.q: Why did Aparna's words help?
qa.a: She gave him permission to feel sad without pushing, which let him drop the act a little.

qa.q: How might the friend in Bengaluru have felt during the weeks without replies?
qa.a: Probably confused and hurt, perhaps thinking Arnab had stopped caring.

grounding: It shows a teenager using detachment over several weeks as a defence against the pain of a friend moving away.

passage: Thomas, when I was sixteen, I failed my pre-board maths exam. Everyone expected me to cry, and I didn't. I told my friends, "Studies are a scam, I don't care." I started coming late, sitting at the back, yawning loudly in class. Teachers thought I'd become lazy. The truth was, I was terrified that if I tried hard and failed again, it would prove I was stupid. Not trying felt safer. It was my cousin who saw through it. She said, "Wasim, you're not bored. You're scared." I was so angry with her. But she was right. I started tuition with her the next week, and I passed.

qa.q: Which exam did young Wasim fail?
qa.a: The pre-board maths exam.

qa.q: Why did young Wasim pretend studies didn't matter?
qa.a: Wasim was terrified that trying and failing again would prove he was stupid, so acting like he didn't care felt safer.

qa.q: What made his cousin's words effective, even though they angered Wasim?
qa.a: She named the fear behind the act, which let Wasim face the real problem and get help.

qa.q: How might Wasim's teachers have seen him differently if they had known?
qa.a: They might have offered encouragement and support instead of seeing him as lazy.

grounding: It shows, told by an elder, a teenager feigning lack of interest in studies to defend against fear of failing again.

passage: The selection list went up on the notice board at 3:55, five minutes before the last bus. Sarika's name wasn't on it. She read it once, shrugged, and said loudly, 'Basketball is boring anyway.' Sunaina, who had been picked, stared at her. There was no time to talk; they ran for the bus, which was packed and roaring with Class 8 boys singing. Squeezed against the door, Sunaina tried: 'You practised every morning for two months.' 'So? Whatever. Doesn't matter.' Sarika put both earphones in and turned to the window. But Sunaina saw her grip the rail so hard her knuckles went pale. At her stop, Sarika got down without saying bye. That night Sunaina texted: 'Not going to pretend it doesn't matter. Call me whenever.'

qa.q: What time did the selection list go up?
What does Sarika gripping the rail suggest, despite her words?
qa.a: It suggests she was hurt and upset, hiding it behind a show of not caring.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do next that respects Sarika's need to protect herself?
qa.a: She could give her space tonight and check in privately later, without forcing her to admit she is hurt. 🤍

qa.q: What might it be like for Sunaina, being picked while her friend wasn't?
qa.a: She may feel happy but guilty, and worried about losing her friend over it.

grounding: Shows a teenager using a show of not caring to shield herself from the pain of rejection, on a crowded rushed journey.

passage: On results morning, the flat in Chennai was too quiet. Amma had lit the lamp twice. Appa kept refreshing the school website on his phone. Harsha, seventeen, sat on the sofa eating cereal slowly. 'Aren't you checking?' asked his brother Kishore, thirteen. 'Why? It's just marks. They don't define anything.' He said it the way he had said it all week, flat and bored. Kishore noticed the cereal had gone soggy and Harsha hadn't taken a bite for ten minutes. When Appa said, 'It's up,' Harsha didn't move. Kishore sat down beside him, close. 'I'll read it first if you want.' Harsha's jaw worked. 'Yeah. Okay. You read it.'

qa.q: How many times had Amma lit the lamp?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: Why was Harsha acting bored about the results?
qa.a: He likely cared a lot and was afraid of being disappointed, so acting detached protected him.

qa.q: What did Kishore get right in how he helped?
qa.a: He didn't argue with Harsha's act; he sat close and offered to read the result first, which let Harsha accept support.

qa.q: How might Amma and Appa read Harsha's flat mood?
qa.a: They might think he truly doesn't care, or see through it, since their own nervousness is obvious.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager feigning indifference to shield himself from a feared disappointment, noticed by his younger brother.

passage:
"So? You made the team list?" asked his cousin Thomas.
"Didn't check," said Sahil, fifteen, scrolling his phone.
"It went up at noon."
"Whatever. Cricket's boring anyway."
"You practised every day for two months."
"So? I was bored."
Thomas sat beside him. "Your name's not on it. I saw."
Sahil's thumb stopped over the screen. For a while the only sound was the ceiling fan. "I know."
"You can be upset."
"I'm not."
"Okay." Thomas waited.
After a long moment, Sahil put the phone face down on the bed. His voice came out smaller than he wanted. "I really thought I'd make it. I even told Nani I would." Thomas nudged his shoulder. "Trials come again in March." Sahil didn't answer, but he didn't say 'whatever' either.

qa.q: When did the team list go up?
qa.a: At noon.

qa.q: Why did Sahil say cricket was boring?
qa.a: He was hurt and disappointed at not making the team, and pretending not to care protected him.

qa.q: What did Thomas do that helped Sahil open up?
qa.a: He stayed, named the truth gently and waited without pushing.

qa.q: How does Thomas see Sahil's "whatever"?
qa.a: He sees through it, knowing Sahil practised hard and must be disappointed.

grounding: Shows a teenager using feigned indifference to hide disappointment, and a cousin gently seeing through it.

passage: I'm Dhruv. When my best friend Gurpreet moved to Canada last year, I told everyone I didn't care. At the farewell, I made jokes and left early. When he messaged from the airport, I replied "ok". My mum asked if I was upset and I said, "People move. It's fine." But I stopped going to the ground where we used to play. It took me months to understand that acting cool was easier than admitting how much I missed him. Last week I finally called him and said, "I miss you, man." He said, "Same." It felt awful and good at once.

qa.q: Where did Gurpreet move to?
qa.a: To Canada.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv act like he didn't care?
qa.a: Dhruv felt deeply sad about losing his friend, and acting cool protected him from that pain.

qa.q: What turning point helped Dhruv?
qa.a: Admitting the truth, that Dhruv missed Gurpreet, and finally calling to say so.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt when Dhruv replied "ok" from the airport?
qa.a: Probably hurt or confused, wondering if Dhruv cared at all.

grounding: Shows a teenager looking back on using detachment to hide sadness about a friend moving away.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Disha, October
Tenzin (14) was sent to me after his teacher noticed he'd stopped handing in homework. When I asked, he shrugged: "Doesn't matter. Nothing matters." He kept his arms folded, but his leg was bouncing. Later he mentioned he'd failed the trials for the school band, which he'd been preparing for all summer. The "I don't care" seems to be a shield. I didn't push. I've arranged a weekly check-in, asked the music teacher to speak with him, and will call his parents to share what I noticed.

qa.q: What trials did Tenzin fail?
qa.a: The trials for the school band.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's bouncing leg suggest despite his shrug?
qa.a: He feels more upset and anxious than he admits, using indifference as a shield.

qa.q: Why is Disha right not to push Tenzin?
qa.a: Pushing might make him defend the shield harder; steady check-ins build trust so he can open up.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's parents feel when Disha calls?
qa.a: Concerned but grateful to understand what's behind his change.

grounding: Shows a young teenager using a show of not caring to protect himself after a disappointment, noted by his counsellor.

passage:

The team list went up. I wasn't on it. Dolma asked if I was okay and I said, "Whatever, cricket's boring anyway." I even laughed. Then I went home and lay on my bed for two hours. passage: In Karad, Rafiq's father announced they were closing the cycle-repair shop and moving to Pune. Rafiq, fifteen, shrugged. "Fine. I don't care." At school, his teacher Minakshi Ma'am mentioned she'd heard. "It's nothing," he said, eyes on his desk. "It's just a shop." But at lunch he went and sat behind the shop, where he'd learned to fix punctures at eight. He ran his hand over the old air pump. Minakshi Ma'am, passing on her scooter, stopped. "You spent your childhood here, na?" Rafiq's throat went tight. "I don't want to cry about a shop." "It's not just a shop," she said. He nodded, finally, and let himself sit there a while.

qa.q: Where was the family moving?
qa.a: To Pune.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he said "It's nothing"?
qa.a: He felt sad and hurt about losing the shop but hid it behind detachment.

qa.q: What did Minakshi Ma'am do that helped Rafiq drop the act?
qa.a: She named what the shop meant to him instead of accepting his "I don't care."

qa.q: How might Rafiq's father feel if he knew how much the shop meant to Rafiq?
qa.a: He might feel touched and sad, and want to talk with his son about the move.

grounding: A small-town teenager feigns indifference about his family's shop closing to cover his sadness.

passage:
When the Tokyo swim club posted the relay team, Aiko's name wasn't on it. She shrugged. "I didn't want to swim relay anyway."
Nkechi, her friend from the changing rooms, raised an eyebrow. "You've been training for it since April."
"It's just swimming. Who cares."
Aiko stopped staying after practice. She scrolled her phone on the bench and said everything was boring. Her coach asked if something was wrong. "Nope. Just over it."
Two weeks later, Nkechi found her crying in the car park. "I care so much it's stupid," Aiko said. "If I act like I don't, it doesn't hurt."
Nkechi sat with her. "It hurts anyway. Might as well have company."
The next morning Aiko asked the coach what she needed to improve.

qa.q: When had Aiko been training for the relay since?
qa.a: Since April.

qa.q: Why did Aiko say it was just swimming and she was over it?
qa.a: She was hurt and embarrassed at being left off, and acting uncaring felt safer than admitting how much it mattered.

qa.q: How could a coach help a swimmer who suddenly acts bored?
qa.a: The coach could gently check in again in private and offer clear steps to improve, so caring feels safe again.

qa.q: What is it like for Nkechi to watch Aiko pretend not to care?
qa.a: Nkechi can see through it and feels concerned, which is why she stays and sits with her.

grounding: Shows a teen masking disappointment with indifference until a friend helps her face it.

"Your class teacher says you've stopped handing in work," said Sangeeta ma'am.

passage:
Dear Sumit,
I owe you an apology for the science exhibition.
When our model collapsed an hour before judging, you were trying to fix it and I just sat there saying "It's only an exhibition, bro, chill." You thought I didn't care. I did. That's the problem.
I had spent three weeks on the wiring. When it fell, I felt so stupid that pretending not to care was easier than admitting I was gutted. So I acted bored and left you to do everything.
I'm sorry. You deserved a partner, not a shrug.
Can we fix it together this weekend and enter the district round? I'll bring the soldering iron and actual effort this time.
Jatin

qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What was Jatin really feeling when the model collapsed?
qa.a: Jatin felt gutted and stupid, and hid it behind acting bored.

qa.q: What was it like for Sumit to see Jatin shrug before judging?
qa.a: Sumit likely felt alone and frustrated, fixing the model while thinking the partner didn't care.

passage: You want to know why I acted like I didn't care, Alka? It's Jeevan you're talking to; you know I care about everything. When the state team list came out and my name wasn't on it, I shrugged in front of everyone. "Football's just a hobby," I said. I stopped going to practice, told people I was busy, even laughed when Coach asked where I'd been. Inside, it felt like someone had switched off a light. It was easier to say "whatever" than to admit I'd trained two years for that list. The day you found my old boots in the bin and fished them out without a word, I nearly broke. I'm back at practice now. It still hurts, but less than pretending did.

qa.q: Where did Alka find Jeevan's old boots?
qa.a: In the bin.

qa.q: What was Jeevan really feeling while saying "Football's just a hobby"?
qa.a: Jeevan felt crushed and hurt, as if a light had been switched off, and the shrug hid that pain.

qa.q: What might have helped Jeevan sooner than pretending?
qa.a: Admitting the disappointment to a friend or to Coach early could have let Jeevan face the setback and return to practice sooner.

qa.q: What is it like for Alka to watch Jeevan act as if nothing matters?
qa.a: Alka likely sees through it and worries, which is why Alka quietly fishes the boots out of the bin.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager faking indifference to hide the hurt of missing a team selection.
